ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text:
As shown in Figure A, a sufficiently long inclined conveyor belt runs counterclockwise at a constant rate. A small slider (considered as a point mass) is gently placed at the top of the conveyor belt. The relationship between the square of the slider's velocity and its displacement on the conveyor belt is shown in Figure B. The magnitude of the gravitational acceleration is taken as $g = 10 \, \mathrm{m/s^2}$.

1. What is the magnitude of the acceleration $a_1$ of the slider within the displacement range of $0 \sim 3.2 \, \mathrm{m}$?
2. What is the magnitude of acceleration $a_2$ of the slider within the displacement range of $3.2 \mathrm{m} \sim 12.2 \mathrm{m}$?
3. What is the coefficient of kinetic friction $\upmu$ between the slider and the conveyor belt?

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: In Figure A, the conveyor belt is placed at an incline, with the upper right end higher; the arrow on the belt surface points along the inclined plane toward the lower left, indicating that the upper surface moves downward along the inclined plane; the small block is placed on the belt surface near the upper end. Figure B is a graph of v^2 versus displacement x; the broken line passes through (0,0), (3.2 m, 64 m^2/s^2), (12.2 m, 100 m^2/s^2), and both segments are straight lines. Reasoning: For uniformly accelerated linear motion, use v^2-v_0^2=2ax, so the slope of the v^2-x graph equals 2a. The slope of the first segment is 64/3.2=20, therefore a1=20/2=10 m/s^2. The slope of the second segment is (100-64)/(12.2-3.2)=36/9=4, therefore a2=4/2=2 m/s^2. Take downward along the inclined plane as the positive direction. Initially, when the block has just been placed on it, its speed is less than the conveyor belt speed, and the friction force is downward along the inclined plane, so a1=g sinθ+μg cosθ. After reaching the turning point, the block reaches the conveyor belt speed; afterward gravity makes it tend to be faster than the conveyor belt, and the friction force is upward along the inclined plane, so a2=g sinθ-μg cosθ. Substitute a1=10, a2=2, g=10: adding gives 12=20 sinθ, sinθ=0.6, so cosθ=0.8; subtracting gives 8=2μ·10·0.8, therefore μ=0.5.
